newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: CIS leaders vow to repel any Afghan border threat.
newsitem.headline: CIS leaders vow to repel any Afghan border threat.

text.p: The Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) has vowed to defend areas bordering on Afghanistan if fighting there spills over. But leaders agreed at a summit meeting not to interfere in the conflict.

Five leaders of former Soviet republics, alarmed by the rise to power in Kabul of a radical Islamic militia, ended their summit on Friday with an appeal to the rival groups to hold talks and for the United Nations to discuss the situation.
"We call upon all warring parties to stop hostilities and resume peace negotiations," Kazakhstan's President Nursultan Nazarbayev said at a joint news conference.
He also accused the Taleban militia of human rights violations after the seizure of Kabul last week, referring to the execution of some of the Taleban's political opponents.
"We denounce the executions and violations of human rights committed in Afghanistan," Nazarbayev said.
The Taleban's victims included former Moscow-backed Afghan president Najibullah, a communist installed as Afghan leader in 1987 during the 10-year Soviet occupation of the country.

Russia and Tajikistan, following up the Almaty summit, agreed on Saturday to tighten security on the Tajik-Afghan border, where Russian frontier guards are helping the pro-Moscow government in Dushanbe resist Islamic Tajik rebels based in Afghanistan.

The summit was attended by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, as well as by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. The CIS is a loose grouping of 12 of the 15 former Soviet states.

Nazarbayev said participants at the summit would take "adequate measures" to defend themselves if the conflict spilled over from Afghanistan. But he and other participants made clear that no practical steps would be taken unless this happened.
"We are strongly against interference in Afghanistan's internal affairs," Nazarbayev said.

Interfax news agency said on Saturday that Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov "agreed to take the necessary measures to strengthen security on the border between Tajikistan and Afghanistan". The agency gave no details.
Russia deploys thousands of border guards along the remote and mountainous border along the Amu Darya river where there are frequent clashes with Tajik Islamist guerrillas.
Uzbek President Islam Karimov said that Afghan warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, was all that stood between the Taleban militia and the former Soviet republics.
Karmimov said that Dostum, who controls a strategic tunnel to the north, deserved stronger support from CIS neighbours.

"If this tunnel is surrendered, they will have no obstacle on their way northwards and we don't know how far they may go," he said. "If we do not want the war to escalate, if we want to force all parties to the negotiating table, we have to make sure that Dostum keeps the tunnel under his control."
There was no indication that the other leaders at the summit shared Karimov's views. Uzbekistan is one of three former Soviet Central Asian republics that border Afghanistan.
Nazarbayev said he, Chernomyrdin, Tajik President Rakhmonov, Uzbekistan's Karimov and Kyrgyzstan President Askar Akayev wanted the U.N. Security Council to meet on Afghanistan.
He also said the five countries would start supplying northern Afghanistan with humanitarian aid.
Chernomyrdin said he thought that the future stand of the CIS states would largely depend on further steps by other countries which have an impact on the situation in Afghanistan.
"We are watching attentively what other countries are doing, including the United States and Pakistan," he said. "This, of course, will influence our position."
